title: Write a `Function<Employee, String>` that extracts the name, then compose it with another function that uppercases using `.andThen(String::toUpperCase)`.
shortTitle: Write a Function<Employee, String> that extracts the name, then compose with andThen(String::toUpperCase)

s1_definition.profdef: `Function<T, R>` maps an input to an output. Its default method `.andThen(after)` composes two functions so the first runs and its result feeds the second. `getName.andThen(String::toUpperCase)` extracts a name then uppercases it.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya first pulls the name off an employee file, then runs that name through a capitaliser. Two steps on an assembly line — get the name, then shout it in capitals.
s1_definition.oneliner: `andThen` chains functions left to right — extract the name, then uppercase it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Function<T, R>` maps an input to an output. Its default method `.andThen(after)` composes two functions so the first runs and its result feeds the second. `getName.andThen(String::toUpperCase)` extracts a name then uppercases it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya first pulls the name off an employee file, then runs that name through a capitaliser. Two steps on an assembly line — get the name, then shout it in capitals.

**One line to remember:** `andThen` chains functions left to right — extract the name, then uppercase it.

sections.s2_technical:
A `Function<Employee, String> getName = Employee::getName` extracts the name. `.andThen(String::toUpperCase)` returns a new function that applies getName first and then applies toUpperCase to its result, yielding a `Function<Employee, String>` that produces an uppercase name.

The order is important: `f.andThen(g)` runs f then g, whereas `f.compose(g)` runs g then f. So andThen reads naturally left to right. The composed function is itself a Function and can be used anywhere one is expected, for example `staff.stream().map(getName.andThen(String::toUpperCase))`.

The senior nuance is that composition builds pipelines of small, testable transformations instead of one big lambda, improving reuse and clarity. You must keep the types aligned — the output of the first function must match the input of the second. For null safety you would insert a mapping step or guard, because toUpperCase on a null name would throw. Choosing andThen versus compose is simply about which function should run first.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A report at the National Bank of India must display employee names in uppercase, and name extraction and uppercasing are two concerns worth composing cleanly.

This is exactly what Function andThen does — it chains the name extractor with the uppercaser into one reusable transformation.

The code defines a `NameFormatService` with the composed function and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: employees named Rajesh and priya.

Step 1: The composed function first applies getName, extracting Rajesh and priya.

Step 2: andThen feeds each name into toUpperCase.

Step 3: The results become RAJESH and PRIYA.

Step 4: map applies the composed function to each employee and toList gathers the uppercase names.

```
INFO: Uppercase names: [RAJESH, PRIYA]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Employee(Rajesh)
    │ getName            → "Rajesh"
    │ andThen toUpperCase→ "RAJESH"
    ▼
  "RAJESH"

  [Rajesh, priya] → map(getName.andThen(toUpperCase)) → [RAJESH, PRIYA]
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Composed Name Formatter ═══

  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ ──names──→ Report
  │ staff    │→│ NameFormatService    │
  │ list     │ │ getName→toUpperCase  │
  └──────────┘ └──────────────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Function.andThen ═══

  ┌─ composition order ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ f.andThen(g): run f FIRST, then g on f's result            │
  │ f.compose(g): run g first, then f (reverse order)          │
  │ getName.andThen(toUpperCase) → Function<Employee,String>   │
  │ types must align: output of f == input of g               │
  │ null name → toUpperCase throws → guard/map if nullable     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │        NameFormatService      │
  │  - upperName: Function         │ getName.andThen(toUpperCase)
  │  + upperNames(List): List      │ map(upperName)
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. stream().map(getName.andThen(toUpperCase))
  2. toList()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Function maps an input to an output, and its default method andThen composes two functions so the first runs and its result flows into the second. I start with a function that extracts the employee name and then call andThen with String toUpperCase, which gives me a single function that extracts the name and then uppercases it, producing an uppercase name for each employee.

The order is the detail interviewers probe: f andThen g runs f first and then g, whereas f compose g runs them in the reverse order. andThen reads naturally left to right, which is why I reach for it here. The composed function is itself a Function, so I can hand it straight to map in a stream, as I do for the uppercase name report at the National Bank of India.

The senior point I stress is that composition lets me build a pipeline of small, individually testable transformations rather than one large lambda, which improves reuse and readability. I just have to keep the types aligned so the output of the first function matches the input of the second, and I add a guard or an intermediate mapping step when a value could be null, because calling toUpperCase on a null name would throw.
